cards.name: Analog gait ladder
cards.summary: Stick magnitude selects one of three cycle animations, and each cycle scales its own playback rate across a band, so ground speed is continuous instead of stepping between walk and run.
cards.behavior: Walking is not a two-way switch. Three cycle animations cover the stick range, and each owns a playback-rate band. Each update the selector reads the stick magnitude: above 3768 it picks the fast cycle, from 2784 to 3768 the middle cycle, and below 2784 the slow cycle. A change of cycle waits until a foot-plant marker of the current cycle has passed, and the new cycle starts at a matching frame, so the stride stays in phase. Inside a cycle the rate is the band minimum at or below the band floor, the band maximum at or above the band ceiling, and a linear interpolation between. The bands are: slow cycle 4096 to 7168 over magnitude 2300 to 2783, middle cycle 3276 to 6144 over 2783 to 3768, and fast cycle 3547 to 4096 over 3768 to 4096. The value 4096 is playback rate 1.0, so the slow cycle runs from 1.0x to 1.75x, the middle from 0.8x to 1.5x and the fast from about 0.87x to 1.0x. While no control flag pauses root translation, each cycle also writes a fixed translation into the root bone: -16, -35 or -60 units on the local forward axis for the slow, middle and fast cycle. The value is multiplied by the rate and by the frame time percentage (100 is one nominal frame), so a faster cycle covers proportionally more ground.

cards.name: Camera-relative bearing
cards.summary: The stick angle is added to the camera's lagged yaw to form the target bearing, so forward on the stick means away from the camera even while the camera is still swinging.
cards.behavior: Movement intent is stored as a bearing in the 4096-unit turn, not in world space. Each update the two stick axes become an angle with an arc tangent, and the camera's lagged yaw is added. The lagged yaw is a copy of the camera yaw that the camera code keeps current, and it is read every update, not latched when the stick is first pressed. A camera that is still swinging therefore keeps rotating the meaning of forward, and the body follows. The sum is stored as the target bearing only while a digital direction code is non-zero. With no direction input the old bearing stays, so the body keeps its last facing. The direction code is built from the pad direction bits. Its eight angle values are written to a local variable that the bearing code never reads, so they do not feed the bearing. This file does not show whether stick motion also sets those bits. The two axes pass through a radial dead zone: when the squared length of the axis pair is below 1024 (a radius of 32 on the plus or minus 128 axis scale), both axes become zero. The magnitude is the vector length times 32, so a full axis value gives 4096, and an axis at plus or minus 128 sets 4096 at once. A non-zero magnitude below 1024 is raised to 1024, a quarter of full. This floor stops a barely touched stick from selecting a useless crawl, because the gait selector reads this magnitude.

constants.name: stickDeadzoneRadius
constants.unit: squared stick units; the dead zone is a radial disk of radius 32 on the plus or minus 128 axis scale

constants.name: stickFullAxisValue
constants.unit: raw axis units; an axis at this value forces full magnitude

constants.unit: magnitude in 4096-unit full-deflection space

cards.name: Rate-limited turning
cards.summary: The body yaw moves toward the bearing by a capped step per update. The step comes from the steering mode, and while walking it shrinks with the angle still to cover.
cards.behavior: Turning never snaps to the requested direction. Each update the body yaw moves toward the bearing by a step, and the move stops exactly on the target instead of overshooting. The step is a per-mode turn rate times the frame time multiplier divided by 4096, so it scales with the frame time. Three modes use a fixed rate: 256 units per update in the turn-in-place state, 96 in the glide state and 64 in the state that grabs and throws. In these three modes, when the angle error is exactly half a turn, the stored target moves by one unit so the body does not oscillate between two equally short arcs. Walking uses a different rule in which the rate follows the size of the angle still to cover. The absolute angular error is measured first. An error above 768 becomes a quarter of itself plus 112. An error at or below 768 gives a flat 112. A small correction turns slowly and precisely, and a half-turn reversal turns at about 624 units per update. The walking rule has no half-turn nudge. The angle error is always wrapped to the shortest arc.

cards.name: Jump as a velocity write
cards.summary: A jump overwrites the vertical and forward speeds outright and sets gravity, so the arc depends on three numbers and not on the speed the body carried.
cards.behavior: A jump does not add an impulse to existing motion. A short crouch state runs first with the physics integrator off. When it ends, the launch writes the velocity out completely and enters a state that waits for the arc to finish. Three launch variants are chosen by the movement mode. The default writes 40 units per update forward and 154 up. One mode writes 83 forward and 154 up, a longer jump. Another mode writes 21 forward and 195 up, a tall and almost vertical leap. All three set gravity to -16 units per update squared. In the default variant, when the movement mode is 16 and the jump button is released during the crouch, the vertical speed is then cut to two thirds, about 102, which gives a short hop. Each variant writes a fixed upward speed, so the apex height does not depend on the approach speed. The jump state hands over to the fall state in two ways. One is the end of the jump animation. The other is a button release, which hands over once the animation frame is more than 4 frames past the frame of the first release, and so cuts a jump short. In movement modes 16 and 32 the release is deferred, and the jump runs to the end of its animation. Landing is a separate state. The ground contact restores normal gravity first. Then it picks a heavy landing animation when the movement mode is the tall-leap mode, when one of three specific animations plays, or when the downward speed is below -256 units per update.

cards.name: Fall, glide and drop
cards.summary: Pressing jump again in the air replaces gravity with a constant forward speed and a slow fixed sink. The velocity ramps over four updates when the pose changes.
cards.behavior: The glide is a velocity override, not a reduced gravity. On entry, when the body is already moving down, the code writes gravity 0, forward speed 52 and vertical speed -24 units per update. The descent is a straight shallow line, and the distance covered depends only on the time aloft. Entry happens when the jump button is pressed again, either in the jump state once its animation reaches frame 2, or in the fall state. A held object of one specific class blocks it. A separate forced-glide state takes over when the body falls inside a level unit flagged as a glide zone. While gliding, a pose change ramps the velocity toward the target (52 forward, or 24 forward in an alternate pose, and -24 down) with a transition force that spreads the change over 4 updates. The glide ends when the button is released and either the glide animation is past frame 12 or another animation plays. Then the code writes gravity back to -16, zero speed, and enters the fall state. The plain fall uses drop physics: acceleration -16 per update squared plus a small forward push of 4. Leaving the ground starts the fall state only when the vertical speed is below a threshold. The threshold is -32 per update by default and -96 during attack states, so a swing can run off a small drop without a fall. The fall continues to accelerate until the per-axis speed clamp of 256 stops it.

constants.unit: engine units per update at the 33 ms nominal frame

cards.name: Trapezoidal body integrator
cards.summary: Every body advances through one routine that adds a half-acceleration term to position and a full term to velocity, then clamps each axis. The player step time follows the animation speed.
cards.behavior: All motion goes through one integrator that uses the constant-acceleration form, not a plain Euler step. The position gains the velocity term plus half of the acceleration term for the step, and only then the velocity gains the full acceleration term. This form is exact for a constant acceleration over the step. Both terms are scaled by an elapsed time in 4096ths of a nominal frame, so 4096 is one update of about 33 ms. For the player, that time is the frame time multiplied by the animation speed adjustment of the first body section, so a faster gait cycle also steps the physics faster. Right after the step, each velocity component is clamped to the body's own per-axis maximum. The player maximum is 256 units per update on all three axes. This clamp is the terminal velocity: under the -16 gravity of a fall, the vertical speed reaches the clamp after 16 updates. The 154-unit jump write starts below the clamp and is never clipped. The integrator runs in physics modes 0 and 4 (forces applied) and in the swim modes. Physics mode 3, used for crouching, wall climbing and landing, has no integrator step, and the animation root translation moves the body. The step is computed in the body's local axes and rotated into the world by a skeleton segment matrix. A flag can drop the vertical part of the step. When the gravity probe snaps the player up to a surface, it moves the body by at most 128 units per response.

cards.name: Streamed world line query
cards.summary: One probe call resolves a start and end pair against the current level, then against other streamed levels, and then against instance groups, and returns a typed hit with the face and its normal.
cards.behavior: Every contact probe in the engine goes through one query that is written for a streaming world. The caller gives a start point, an end point and a mask of what may be hit. The default mask for general probes is 63, with every bit set. Bit 1 enables terrain. Bit 8 sweeps instance groups 16 to 31. Bit 16 together with bit 2 or bit 4 sweeps two tables of 8 groups each, and bit 4 alone sweeps a third table. The terrain pass runs first against the level the body stands in. It returns the face that was crossed, the tree node that holds it and the face normal, and the query reports a terrain hit with all three. If the current level gives nothing, the routine scans 16 streamed unit slots. It skips the slots that are not fully loaded and the level it already tested. When the current level is a warp room and the test missed, it also skips other warp-room levels. A probe near a level boundary therefore finds the floor on the other side. After the terrain pass, whether or not it hit, the mask bits drive the sweep of the instance lists. Each instance first passes a cheap test: the point of the segment nearest to the instance must lie inside a quarter of its bounding radius squared. Only then does the full model test run. Instances with a no-collide flag are skipped. The caller marks the probing body and its children so they do not hit themselves. The normal comes from the shared terrain normal list, unless the world is mid-morph. In that case a normal is rebuilt from the face vertices.

constants.unit: bitmask of hit categories, all six bits set

cards.name: Ledge detection and grab
cards.summary: A chain of line probes looks for a wall below head height and a near-flat lip just above it, and the surface normals decide whether the body commits to the grab.
cards.behavior: Edge detection is a probe sequence, not one ray. It runs only while the grab control flag is set and no heavy held object blocks it. First, a horizontal probe at 544 units above the body origin (the 400 rise plus 144) reaches 256 units forward. If it hits nothing, a vertical probe checks the headroom from 144 up to 128 units above that point. If either one hits, the wall is taller than a grabbable ledge and the attempt stops, unless the high probe found a wall that the body can climb. Next, a second horizontal probe at 400 units above the origin reaches 256 units forward. It counts only if the face normal has a vertical component below 2048 in the 4096-unit scale, a face steeper than about 60 degrees. A lip probe then starts 144 units above that wall hit, a little past the wall face, and runs down. It needs a top surface with a vertical normal of at least 3548, which is nearly flat. The commit test also asks for more than 2896, but any normal that passes 3548 already passes it, so the second test never rejects. The ledge top is therefore between 400 and 544 units above the body origin. On a commit, the velocity is set to zero. A response routine rotates the body to face the wall normal and moves it so that a hang point 196 units forward and 498 units above the body origin lands on the ledge edge. The probe sizes are fixed, so tall and short bodies use the same reach.

cards.name: Slope slip and slide
cards.summary: One normal threshold separates floor from slope. On a slope the gravity probe samples a point further downhill, and the forward move is projected onto the plane underfoot.
cards.behavior: The boundary between ground and slope is a surface normal, not an angle. A face counts as ground only while its vertical normal component is at or above 2896 of 4096, about 45 degrees. A face with a normal between 0 and 2896 is too steep. In that case the gravity probe finds the downhill direction from the face normal and probes a second point displaced down the slope. The displacement is the downhill vector times the larger of the current downward speed and 48, divided by 4096. If the second face is also too steep, a slide flag is set. The response then moves the body along x and y by the probe offset, and a slide event is posted. If the second face is acceptable, the body x and y snap to the new point, so a short steep patch nudges the body downhill and does not slide it. Separately, a movement check projects the intended forward vector onto the plane of the face underfoot. It takes the dot product with the normal, divides by 4096 and subtracts that share of the normal. What remains is the part along the plane, so a body walking onto a slope follows the surface and does not stop dead or lift off. The same slip threshold also feeds the drop-off probe. A separate floor query in the drop-height probe accepts a hit only when the normal is above 3200.

constants.unit: normal units in 4096-unit scale, where 4096 is straight up

cards.name: Wall crawling
cards.summary: The wall-climb state turns the integrator off and re-pins the body to the face every update with two probes, and steering switches to a frame measured on the wall.
cards.behavior: Climbing is a physics mode of its own. The state sets the physics mode to 3, which has no integrator step, so gravity does not act. A wall-follow routine runs every update in its place. It runs two probes along the root bone local axes. The first starts 64 units off the root and reaches 448 units along the local axis that points at the surface. It records the surface normal, builds the body rotation that aligns with that normal, and computes the position correction that holds the body 186 units off the surface along the normal. A second probe, offset 160 units along the surface from the first and slightly longer, records a second normal. The angle between the two normals gives an extra pitch when both probes hit, so the body follows convex and concave bends. Repeating the test each update lets the body follow a curved surface, not one plane. The position shift applies only when its squared length is above 100. This removes the jitter from small errors on a flat face. The world rotation controller is driven from the first normal, so one pose lies flat on a wall, floor or ceiling. When neither probe hits, the climb ends: the body rotation is cleared and the state returns to idle. Steering on the wall differs. The bearing is the difference between the wall frame yaw minus a half turn and the stick direction, because the climb pose is rotated onto the face.

cards.name: Water depth bands and swim steering
cards.summary: Depth thresholds around the water plane mark wading, treading and swimming, and swimming steers with independent yaw and pitch rates instead of a bearing.
cards.behavior: Water is not a boolean state. The water probe reports separate condition bits and edge signals. The depth of the body reference point below the water plane is compared with two thresholds. A tread bit is set when that point is under the surface by less than 112 units. A deep-swim bit is set when it is under by more than 256 units. While swimming, a further probe reaches down 4 times 416 units to measure the water column. A wade bit is set while the measured water depth is under 416 units, and it stays clear when the water is deeper. Edge bits report crossing the surface in either direction and passing the swim depth while moving down. The probe is run with a fixed set of three numbers, so the same thresholds apply to every body that uses it. A body can be well over a stride under the surface and still be classed as wading. Once the swim state takes over, the stick does not produce a bearing. The horizontal stick part turns the yaw at 32 units per update times the sine of the stick angle. The vertical part changes a separate pitch offset at 48 units per update times the cosine, so vertical aiming is faster than turning. The pitch offset is clamped between 0 and 2048, a half turn. The step is scaled by the frame time multiplier. In the plane whose index is 1, a drain is applied every update while the body has a water face and lacks the swim ability. Its weight is 40960 in 4096ths, which is 10, and the plane rate table scales it. Getting out of the water stops it.

constants.unit: engine units below the water plane

cards.name: Capped-damper follow camera
cards.summary: The follow camera eases its distance and focus point toward targets with a capped damper, and the distance ease is fast when a wall pushes in and slow when it relaxes.
cards.behavior: The follow camera never sits at a fixed offset from the character. A damper moves each tracked value. Every update it replaces the velocity with a fixed fraction of the remaining error and adds that velocity to the value. The fraction is one quarter in the default mode, one half in the fast mode and one eighth in the slow mode. A cap limits the step. Only when the step hits the cap is it scaled by the frame time multiplier. The result is an exponential ease per update, not a true second-order spring, and it is not frame-rate independent below the cap. The distance damper picks its mode from the collision result. When a wall shortens the target below the preferred distance, the fast mode runs with cap 512. When the target is shorter than the current distance but not shortened by a wall, the default mode runs with cap 128. When the target is farther than the current distance, the slow mode runs with cap 64. The camera therefore pulls in fast and eases back out slowly. The focus point speed cap is recomputed every update from the gap between the focus point and its target plus a floor of 20 units, or a hundredth of the distance if larger. A forced camera move multiplies the floor by five. The start value of 200 only applies at initialization. The vertical focus uses a separate damper, described in the collision card. Distances come from a table with three groups of three slots, picked by camera mode group and a preset index. The first group holds 1500, 2250 and 3200 units. The second holds 1500, 2000 and 2600. The tightest group holds 1200, 1600 and 2000. The start state uses the middle slot of the first group, 2250. The focus point is 352 units above the player origin and 512 above any other instance, so the camera aims at the chest.

cards.name: Pull-in on obstruction
cards.summary: Up to four sweep lines from the focus point decide the camera response: a blocked side line swings the yaw, another blocked line shortens the distance, and a full block snaps the distance. A vertical damper keeps the focus from bobbing.
cards.behavior: Camera collision treats the camera as a sphere of radius 280 units, swept from the focus point toward the wanted camera position along up to four test lines. The set of lines alternates between updates. The follow camera reads the result by which lines are blocked. When all four are blocked, the target distance is the measured sweep length. When only one of the two side lines (the first two line slots) is blocked, the camera does not pull in. The target yaw swings away from the obstacle, and a step of 64 units is used when the line angle is large. When one of the other two lines is blocked, the target distance is set to the measured length through a debounce routine. A separate underwater camera uses a simpler rule. It takes the measured length minus a 150-unit margin and floors the result at 400 units, so a swimmer pressed against a wall still gets a usable view. The vertical focus has its own damper with unequal step caps. When the focus is above its target, which means the body moved down, the step cap is one sixth of the remaining error while the camera mode flags for airborne states are set and the real focus is above the recorded fall height. Otherwise the cap is twice the error, which is almost no cap. When the focus is below its target, the cap is one sixth of the error, raised to at least 50 in one mode. Errors under 5 units are ignored. So the camera does not dive after a falling body. The start projection is 320 units with a near plane of 50 and a far plane of 12000. Changing the projection distance rebuilds the view volume and re-derives the fog range of every streamed level.

constants.name: cameraSphereRadius
constants.unit: engine units

cards.name: Combat framing
cards.summary: While a target is engaged, the focus point slides between the two bodies in fixed steps, and the camera backs off only as far as the player's screen offset demands.
cards.behavior: Combat framing reuses the follow rig and bends two of its inputs. The focus point becomes a weighted average of the engaged target position and the player position. The weight is the share given to the player, and 4096 means the player alone. The weight moves in fixed steps inside a window from 2048 to 4096. It rises by 48 per update while the player's projected row is below 240 on the 240-row screen and falls by 48 per update while that row is above 210. So the blend follows where the player is drawn on screen. Distance comes from the player's horizontal screen offset from the center column 256. That offset in pixels is multiplied by the projected depth and divided by 128, capped at 3000 units, and never below the ordinary follow distance. The camera backs off only when the player's projection drifts from the center of the frame. Tilt comes from the on-screen angle between the two bodies. The absolute angle is folded into a range of 0 to 1024, divided by 8, and the result is subtracted from a bias of -170. A target to one side tilts the camera a little. When nothing is engaged, the distance becomes the ordinary follow distance and the weight is set to 4096. When the combat mode flag is off, the weight is reset to 2048.

cards.name: Engagement cone and distance windows
cards.summary: What the action button can address is chosen per object ability with its own distance window, and some abilities add a wide cone test. The nearest candidate per category wins.
cards.behavior: The game decides what the player addresses with per-ability tests, not a lock-on. A candidate with the first ability bit (climb or grab type) needs a horizontal distance under 512 units and a vertical offset between -256 and 640. It has no cone test. When the player is in the swim mode, both distances are halved first. A candidate with ability bit 2, 4 or 8 that is not hidden must first pass a cone test, then a line check. The cone uses a half angle of 967 in the 4096-unit turn, about 85 degrees, on the horizontal axis and on the elevation, so a target does not need to be centered, but an object behind the player is rejected. The line check sends a 320-unit probe ahead of the player and fails when it hits terrain. After both tests, abilities 2 and 4 use a horizontal distance under 640 and a vertical offset between -16 and 16, a flat window at the character's own height. Ability 8, a collectible, uses 525 horizontally and -256 to 256 vertically. Switch-type objects carry their own distance and cone data in a property table. Each category keeps one slot, and a new candidate replaces the stored one only when it is closer. The charged-blade target query uses the same cone but a distance under 3200 units.

cards.name: Table-driven melee chain
cards.summary: Each swing is a table row with its own animation, ignore delay and power scale. A button press after the ignore delay chains to the next row at the end of the animation.
cards.behavior: Melee is table driven from the first frame. An attack index selects a row list, and the held object adds an offset of 1 to 4 to the index, so the same button gives a different swing with empty hands, a light object, a heavy object or the charged blade. A row supplies the animation, the blend-in frames, an effect ribbon, an ignore delay in animation frames, a power scale, a knockback distance and a knockback frame count. The row values live in a data table that the code reads, so they are not in the source. Damage is not read from the animation. A weapon or hand collision raises a contact message, and the power it carries is multiplied by the row power scale in 4096ths before it goes to the target, with the body hit by the previous swing in the same message. Chaining needs a new button press. A press that arrives once the animation frame is at or past the ignore delay sets a buffered flag. At the end of the animation, if the flag is set and the next row is not empty, the state moves to the next row and its animation. A press before the ignore delay is dropped. With no buffered press, the state returns to idle, to auto-face or to movement. Two timers attach to specific cases. Attack indices of 10 and above, with an engaged target, hold an auto-facing mode for 4 frames, and attack index 5 sets a one-frame timer. When a swing ends, the code sets the fall-entry speed threshold to -96, three times the default, so a swing at a small drop does not drop into the fall state.

cards.name: Blade charge cycle
cards.summary: While the blade is charged a countdown and a rumble ramp run together, and the cycle re-arms itself on a fixed period instead of ending.
cards.behavior: The charged blade runs its own timer, counted down by the frame time multiplier, and while the timer is non-zero the controller rumble is re-armed every update, not started once. The rumble strength comes from a separate accumulator that climbs by the frame time multiplier up to a cap of 245759. Below the cap the strength is the accumulator divided by 4096 plus a base of 50. Above it the strength is pinned at 110. So the motor ramps from 50 to 110 over 60 nominal updates, about two seconds, then holds. Each update the pad is re-armed with a 20480 duration, so a long charge does not fall silent partway. When the countdown reaches zero the effect does not stop. A full 61440 is added back to the timer and a blast ring is fired, so the visual pulse repeats every 15 nominal updates for as long as the blade stays charged. Cancelling zeroes the timer and the accumulator, stops the motor and ends the instance effects in one call.

cards.name: Health counter and plane transfer
cards.summary: One health integer serves both planes, but its ceiling, its drain or regeneration and its floor differ. Dropping below 100000 in plane 1 forces the move to the other plane.
cards.behavior: Both planes share one health integer, and the rules differ by plane. In plane 1 the maximum is the number of health upgrades plus one, times 100000. Each update the integer changes by a rate from a tuning table, scaled by the frame time. That table is data, so its sign is not visible in the source. The water drain also adds to it, with a weight of 10 in 4096ths. When the integer drops below 100000, the body shifts to the other plane and an invincibility timer starts. Above 100000 and below 150000 is a warning band. A countdown falls by 1000 per nominal update, and when it passes zero it reloads with the excess over 100000, floored at 18750. It then fires a power ring and a rumble. A smaller excess therefore pulses faster. In plane 2 the integer is bounded at 100000. A tuning rate moves it toward that value from below, and it is set to 100000 from above. Below 525 the state switches to an idle reaction animation, the integer is set to 525 and a control flag is set. Below zero, which the flag normally prevents, the integer resets to 50000 and a plane change is requested. A hit lowers health only while the integer is above 525, no invulnerability flag is set, and the invincibility timer is zero. The change is the damage value times 20000 divided by 4096, so a hit of 4096 is worth 20000 units. The same scale applies to a health gain, which is capped at the plane 1 maximum. After a hit, the invincibility timer is set from a tuning value times 122880.

cards.name: Free-look head offset
cards.summary: The look input drives an upper-body aim offset with asymmetric limits and does not move the camera directly.
cards.behavior: In the few states that allow it, the look input does not orbit the camera. It accumulates a head and torso offset that is layered on the playing animation. Pad axis 4 is divided by 4 and axis 3 by 3 before they are added to the pitch and yaw offsets. Yaw is therefore a third faster than pitch for the same travel. The code does not say which physical stick these axes are. While a throw is charged, the divisors are 8 and 6, so the aim is slower. The offset is wrapped into the signed half-turn range and clamped. The pitch is limited to -768 and 512, and the yaw to plus or minus 1024, a quarter turn. The clamped offset goes to three additive skeleton controllers (ids 14, 16 and 17) at 50, 30 and 20 percent, so the whole upper body turns. Releasing the look interpolates the three controllers away with a ramp value of 300, so the pose returns smoothly. The look is allowed only while the body is idle on the ground, mid-throw, or swimming.
